page_title: Writing automated tests for your documentation

sources.entry: Writing automated tests for your documentation: this should be required, IMO. Testing code samples in your documentation ensures they never get outdated.

summary.title: Writing automated tests for your documentation
summary.one_liner: Learn how to write automated tests for documentation, such as validating file names, page headers, image assets, tool-name spelling, and code samples, using fastlane's docs setup as an example.
takeaways: Documentation can be tested like code: check file naming, page headers, image paths, and spelling conventions in CI.
Code samples can be extracted and verified against the latest release, catching syntax errors, unknown actions, wrong parameter names, and wrong parameter types.
Run docs tests both on each software release and on each documentation change so regressions block merges.
summary.summary: The author explains why documentation should be tested: docs drift from APIs, code samples contain typos, and releases can cause regressions. Using fastlane's docs site (Markdown converted to HTML with MkDocs) as the example, the post shows Ruby lane snippets that check lowercase file names, require a header on each page, and enforce tool-name formatting. It then describes verifying code samples for syntax errors, existing actions, valid parameter names, and parameter types, noting this found 28 errors in the actions docs. Tests are recommended to run on release deploys and on docs CI.
